appraisal_events.evidence: « C’était bien les de Cambremer, n’est-ce pas ?… C’est une marquise. Et authentique. Pas par les femmes. » ; « c’est une femme bien simple, elle est charmante, on ne fait pas moins de façons » ; « nous restons cachés, comme l’humble violette » ; « maintenant que vous traitez des marquises ! »
appraisal_events.explanation: The hotel bourgeois treat the Cambremer marquise as the apex of the local social world: her title is verified as genuine, her manner praised, and mere proximity to her makes the bâtonnier « chic ». The narrator ironizes the admirers — the offered introduction is likened to Assuérus offering Esther half his kingdom — but the irony falls on their awe, not on her rank, which the passage leaves intact.

status_effects.explanation: Within this scene she is the unquestioned social summit: her marquisate is authenticated (« authentique. Pas par les femmes »), an introduction to her is staged as a royal gift, and having lunched with her is what makes a host « chic ».
Beyond rank she is personally well spoken of — « une femme bien simple », « charmante », making no fuss — so the local appraisal of her character is positive as well.

ambiguities: « les de Cambremer » / « une marquise » does not disambiguate between Mme de Cambremer née Legrandin and the dowager marquise de Cambremer, whom the reference sheet flags as sharing the surface form « marquise de Cambremer »; the annotation attaches the movement to Mme de Cambremer, but the elevated referent could be the dowager.

The passage's other central movement is the narrator's ironic diminishment of the unnamed bâtonnier (his transparent boasting, the Assuérus/Esther simile, his bravado « enhardi maintenant que le danger était passé »); he is an unnamed descriptor figure absent from the reference sheet, so that movement is not recorded as an event, which makes this annotation one-sidedly positive relative to the passage's comic force.
